2. The short facts relevant for the purpose of disposal of this rule are that Hussain Mohammad Ershad the respondent No. 1 was elected as member of Parliament (Jatiya Sangsad) in the general election held on 12.0.96 from 21 Rangpur-3 Constituency. After he laid down the office of the President of the country the Bureau of Anti-Corruption started several criminal cases against him for the offences of criminal misconduct involving moral turpitude under section 5(I) and (2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 (Act 11 of 1947). The Special Case No.7 of 1991 arising out of Ramna P.S. Case N. 4(1)91 against the respondent No. 1 regarding cash of taka 1.90 crores having been recovered from his residence. The respondent No. 1 was convicted in that case and was sentenced to suffer imprisonment for 3 (three) years for the offence of misconduct punishable under section 5(2) read with section 5(1)(e) of the said Act of 1947. Against the said order of conviction and sentence the respondent preferred Criminal Appeal No. 173 of 1992 before this Division. The Special Case No. 19 of 1993 arising out of Ramna P.S. Case No. 96(7)91 was started against the respondent No. 1 and in that case he was convicted and sentenced to suffer imprisonment for 3 years and to pay a fine of Taka. 10,000/00, in default to suffer imprisonment for another 4 months of his being found guilty of misconduct under section 5(1)(d) of Act II of 1947. Against the said order of conviction, the respondent No. 1 preferred Criminal Appeal No. 1472 of 1995 in the High Court Division and the order of stay was granted. 

 3. Another 'Special Case No. 11 1992 arising out of Motijheel P.S. Case No. 48(4)91 which is commonly known as Janata Tower Case was started against the respondent No. 1 and in that case also he was convicted and sentenced to undergo a simple imprisonment for 7 years for committing offences of criminal misconduct under section 5(1)(d) and 5(1)(e) of Act II of 1947 by judgment and order dated 7.6.93 passed by the learned Additional Sessions Judge, 2nd Court and ex-officio, Special Judge, Dhaka and against which the respondent No. 1 filed Criminal Appeal No. 1132 of 1993 in this Division. And after hearing, this Division upheld the aforesaid order of conviction and sentence by reducing the sentence of 7 (seven) years to 5 (five) years simple imprisonment and also to pay fine of taka 5,48,70,800/00, in default, to suffer imprisonment for two years more by judgment and order dated 24.8.2000. Against the said order of conviction the respondent No. 1 filed a Criminal Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 226 of 2000 before the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court and the Appellate Division dismissed the Leave Petition reducing the substantive sentence of 5 years passed by the High Court Division to the period already undergone by the respondent No. 1 and maintained the order of fine of Taka 5,48,70,800/00 (Five core forty eight lacs, seventy thousand eight hundred) in default to suffer simple imprisonment for 6(six) months only. The petitioner's case is that in view of the aforesaid order of conviction and sentence for the offence of criminal misconduct involving moral turpitude respondent No. 1 has been disqualified from being Member of Jatiya Sangsad by reason of provisions of Article 62(2)(d) and 67(I)(d) of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh as such the respondent No. 1 is not entitled to hold or continue to hold the post of Member of Parliament or to sit or attend in any proceeding of the Parliament. The respondent No. 2 and 3 are duty bound under the law to take notice of disqualification of respondent No. 1 and to act in accordance with law. 

 6. The Rule is resisted by the respondent No. 1 by filing affidavit-in-opposition where in it has been stated that the criminal cases were filed against him to victimise him politically and in none of the cases he was convicted for offences involving moral turpitude and as such it does not attract the provision of disqualification under the Constitution. The filing of the writ petition is with malafide intention as the same has been filed after long lapse of 8/9 years only to serve the political purpose of Mr. Anwar Hossain Manju who being behind the screen got this writ petition filed as benamdar of the petitioners. The petitioners are not aggrieved persons and their fundamental rights have not been infringed in any way. The Rule is liable to be discharged for all the above reasons. 

 8. Mr. Rokonuddin Mahmud the learned Counsel appearing for the petitioners, having taken us through the writ petition, supplementary affidavit of the petitioner and the affidavit-in-opposition of the respondent No. 1 made several submissions before us. The learned Counsel has firstly contended that admittedly the High Court Division in Criminal Appeal No. 1132 of 1993 convicted and sentenced the respondent No. 1 to suffer simple imprisonment for 5(five) years and to pay a fine of taka 5,48,70,800/00 (Taka Five Crore forty eight lac, seventy thousand eight hundred) in default to suffer for a further period of 2(two) years and the said order of conviction and sentence was upheld by the Appellate Division with modification of sentence holding that the respondent No. 1 has already suffered 3 years and 6 months imprisonment and his sentence was reduced to the period already undergone but the payment of fine was maintained and in default to pay he will have to suffer simple imprisonment for 6 months only. The learned Counsel has pointed out that the Appellate Division found that the former President the respondent No. 1 abused his position as the President and obtained pecuniary advantage for himself and others and thereby committed offence of criminal misconduct under section 5(1)(d) and also found that the payment of taka 6 ½  (six and half crore) for construction of building being disproportionate to his known sources of income is also an offence punishable under section 5(1)(e) of the Prevention of Corruption Act 1947 (Act II of 1947). Mr. Rokonuddin Mahmud has, therefore, emphatically argued that in view of the aforesaid order of conviction and sentence the respondent No. 1 is disqualified from being member of Parliament and ceased to be such member under the provision of Article 66 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh and his seat is liable to be vacated under the provision of clause 1(d) of Article 67 of the said Constitution. The provision of the said Article 66 and 67 are quoted below: 

 9. In course of his further argument Mr. Rokonuddin Mahmud pointed out that according to Black's Law Dictionary the word moral' pertains to character, conduct, intention, social relations etc. and 'moral turpitude' means the act of business vileness or the depravity in private and social duties which man owes to his fellow man, or to society in general contrary to accepted and customary rule of right and duty between man and man. In another dictionary meaning he pointed the meaning of the term moral concerned with goodness and badness of character or disposition or with the distinction between right and wrong, virtuous in general conduct. Referring to the different meanings of the word 'moral' and 'moral turpitude', Mr. Rokonuddin Mahmud contends that the nature of offences committed by a person not less than a former President of the country has shocked the moral conscience of the society in general and he has been looked down upon by the people. His conduct is being contrary to honesty and integrity of his character and it amounts to moral turpitude of highest decree. In order to strengthen his above argument Mr. Rokonuddin Mahmud has placed reliance in the case of Risal Singh, petitioner Chandgi Ram and others respondents reported in AIR 1966 Punjab 393. In that case the sole question for decision was whether the conviction of Chandgi Ram respondent No. 1 under section 19(f) of the Indian Arms Act for being in possession of an unlicensed revolver can be considered within the meaning of S.153 of Delhi Land Reform Act 1954 (Act No. 8 of 1954) to be a conviction of an offence involving moral turpitude so as to disentitled him to be elected to or to remain a member of the Goan Panchayet. Their Lordships of the Division Bench while 

 "On the facts of the case before us we are unable to find any error in the view of the learned Single Judge that the offence for which Chandgi Ram respondent was convicted implied no such depravity and wickedness of character or disposition which would involve any moral turpitude. As observed by the learned Single Judge, people keep-fire-arms for their personal safety and some time they resort to keeping arms without a licence when they feel that their status in society is not such as would enable them to get a licence from the authority. No doubt they commit a contravention of the law, but it can not necessarily be postulated that this convention involved moral depravity ana ness of character." 

 10. Mr. Rokonuddin Mahmud also argued that although the said decision may not look apparently applicable in the instant case but he relied on the said decision on the question of test which should ordinarily be applied fc judging whether a certain offence did or did not involve moral turpitude.  13. Mr. Rafique-ul-Hoq the learned Counsel appearing for the respondent No. 1, on the other hand, contended that the order of conviction and sentence as passed against his client, does not involve moral turpitude and on similar ground the Additional Secretary Jatiya Sangsad issued on 30.8.2000 declaring his seat vacant as member of Parliament. Against the said order this respondent No. 1 filed Writ Petition No. 4569 of 2000 and obtained an order of stay from this Division. Mr. Hoq, therefore, contents since there arises a dispute regarding the qualification or disqualification of a member of Parliament after his election under Article 66(4) of the Constitution read with Article 70 of the Constitution, the dispute shall be referred by the Speaker to the Election Commission under Rule 178 of the Rules of Procedure of Parliament of Bangladesh, 1974 (modified upto 1981) and unless and until the forum has not been exhausted by the petitioners as an alternative remedy this writ petition is not maintainable. Mr. Hoq, has referred to the case of Khandaker Delwar Hossain and another V. Speaker of Bangladesh Jatiyo Sangsad (Parliament) and another reported in 51 DLR (HC)1 which was affirmed by the Appellate Division as reported in Volume 4 of Bangladesh Law Chronicles at page 273. The facts of the above cited case and those of present case are quite distinguishable and the same cannot be applied in this case. 

 14. The next question raised by the learned Counsel that the petitioners are not aggrieved persons and as such they have no locus standi to file this application. We are unable to accept this contention because under Article 102(2) does not require that the applicant for a writ of quo-warranto must be an aggrieved party as has been decided in the case of Dr. Kamal Hossain V. Serajul Islam, reported in 21DLRSC23. A reference may also be made in the case of Farid Mia V. Amjad Ali reported in 42 DLR(AD) 13 wherein their Lordships of the Appellate Division held as follows:- 

 "The election of a candidate could not be challenged under Article 102 of the Constitution but when the candidate after being elected assumes the office of Chariman or other public office then any persons can invoke the provision of sub-Article (b)(ii) of the Article 102 requiring him to under what authority he claims to hold that Office. It is well known that the jurisdiction under the aforesaid provision amounts to what in England used to be known as prerogative exercise of the writ of quo warranto. In England since 1938 or information’s in the nature quo' warranto were abolished and it was provided that, in any case where a person acted in an office in which he was not entitled to act and an information in the nature of quo warranto would have lain against him, the High Court might the instance of any person who would have been entitled to apply for such an information, grant an injunction restraining the former from so acting and might (if the case so required) declare the office to be vacant. (Halsbury's Law of England, Third Edition Volume II Page 145 Para 273." 

 15. We therefore hold that anyone can file a writ of quo warranto as it is the public duty of citizens to demand removal of all usurpers in public interest. On the question of locus standi a reference may also be made to the case of Vidya Sagar Singh V. Krisha Ballabha Sahey and others reported in AIR 1965 Patna 321. Wherein their Loardships held in the following language. 

 "Before I conclude, I may advert to an objection taken by the learned Attorney General regarding the locus standi of the petitioner to file this application for a writ in the nature of quo warranto. It was urged by him that the petitioner was in no way connected with the legislature and only because he chooses to describe himself as a social worker, he cannot be permitted to question the nomination, as he has no personal interest in the matter, nor has he been prejudiced by these nominations. I do not, however, consider this argument as valid, for dismissing the application on this preliminary ground. In my opinion there is no bar to the petitioner agitating the questions of p importance which have been raised in this case. Be that as it may, I have held that the petitioner has failed to substantiate contention that opposite parties Nos. 3-7 have not been nominated to the legislation Counsel by the Governor of Bihar, and therefore, must fail and it is dismiss with costs. 

 16. From the above cited decision we are of the view that the writ petition is maintainble and the objection regarding alternative remedy cannot also be raised under the fat and circumstances of the instant case. 

 17. Mr. Rafique-ul-Hoq, the learned Counsel has also taken an exception with regard to the very filing of this application after a long delay of 8(eight) years and it is a malafide. The question of malafide is a dispute question of fact. He who alleges malafide must prove it, this is the law. However, we do not find any such material on record to hold as such. Regarding the question of delay we may also refer to the case of Md. Hanif and others V. Chamari Sao and others reported in AIR1965 Allahabad 151 wherein the learned Single Judge held that there can be no question of delay in presenting a petition for writ of quo warranto in which the right of a perse to function in a certain capacity is challenges Every day a fresh cause of action arises on the theory of "De die in diem" that means front day to day. So we hold that no application for quo warranto can be dismissed for any length of delay.
